fetched_contents.text: Bioleaching of gold from waste printed circuit boards by alkali-tolerant Pseudomonas fluorescens Introduction In recent years, as the amount of discarded electronic devices continue to be increased, environmental issues related to electronic waste (e-waste) have received great attention. Globally, 44.7 million tons of e-waste was produced in 2016, and it is estimated that the number will reach 52.2 million tons by 2021, growing at a rate of 3% to 4% per year (Balde et al., 2017). Electronic waste has been considered as a “secondary ore” in “urban mining” resulting from higher metals content than that in primary ores (Kumar et al., 2018). The mobile phone is one of the major contributors of e-waste (Hira et al., 2017). Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are the largest source of valuable and hazardous metals (Yazici and Deveci, 2013; Willner et al., 2015), which contain more than 60 elements (Tansel, 2017; Khaliq et al., 2014; Vats and Singh, 2015). According to estimation, there are ~350 g gold (Au), ~1380 g silver (Ag), ~210 g palladium (Pd), ~130 kg copper (Cu), contained in one tonne of waste mobile phones (Hsu et al., 2019). The dominating economic value of recovering waste mobile phones lies in the recycling of gold. Quanyin et al. (2017) reported that Au and Ag content of each PCB in the waste mobile phone are 0.86 mg/g to 1.60 mg/g and 0.14 mg/g to 5.8 mg/g, respectively. Meanwhile, from 2010 to 2015, the proportion of recycled Au in global Au production will continuously increase with a rate of 0.07–0.19% and the recycled gold could meet 10% of the total gold demand (Quanyin et al., 2017). An analysis by Guo and Yan (2017) showed that the total weight of waste mobile phones produced in one year will exceed 140 Gg in 2025, and the total weight of precious metals such as Ag, Au contained in waste mobile phones will reach 56,250 kg and 28,130 kg, respectively. Thus, there has been increased interest in waste mobile phones recycling, especially to recover precious metals from waste printed circuit boards. Recovering metals from Waste printed circuit boards (WPCBs) is of great significance in terms of resources, environment and economy. Current control technologies for gold recovery from e-waste include pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, mechanical separation and biometallurgy (Syed, 2012; Ning et al., 2017). Pyrometallurgical processes are defined by their use of incineration, smelting, combustions and pyrolysis in a furnace or blast furnace at high temperatures (Jingying et al., 2015; Sheel and Pant, 2017), which is not regarded as an advisable method resulting in the high energy consumption and pollution to the atmosphere. Hydrometallurgical process makes use of cyanide, halide, thiourea and thiosulfate to recycle metals in acidic or alkaline solvent (Pant et al., 2012). However, hydrometallurgical process for recovering metals consumes large amounts of chemical reagents, produces a variety of by-products, and generates high volumes of effluents (Arshadi and Mousavi, 2014; Narayanasamy et al., 2018). Bioleaching technology has been regarded as a promising technology for recycling metals due to the superiorities of environmental friendliness and low-cost (Zhihui et al., 2018). With the progress of the research on gold leaching technology, the hydrometallurgical processes have been replaced gradually by biometallurgical processes (bioleaching) in the mining industry (Das et al., 2011; Yi et al., 2011a, Yi et al., 2011b; Yuguang et al., 2017), which are also applied to recover valuable metals from e-waste (Baoping et al., 2009, Baoping et al., 2012; Priya and Hait, 2017). It is worth mentioning that cyanidation, one of the hydrometallurgy process, is widely used in metals recycling due to its high leaching efficiency and low operating cost. At present, new microbial leaching method is being considered, in order to replace traditional cyanide leaching method (Jingying et al., 2015), especially cyanogenic bacteria, including Chromobacterialum violaceum, Pseudomonas fluorescens, Pseudomons plecoglossicida, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Bacillus megaterium and fungi such as Polysporus sp. and Clitocybe sp. (Brandl and Faramarzi, 2006, Brandl et al., 2008; Chi et al., 2011; Jingying et al., 2015; Arshadi and Mousavi, 2015, Arshadi et al., 2016; Jujun et al., 2014). They all can produce CN− which serves as lixiviant. Gold cyanidation is an electrochemical process in which gold is dissolved in the alkaline cyanide solution and forms gold cyanide complex (Franco et al., 2016). Cyanide-producing bacteria produce cyanide during oxidative decarboxylation of glycine (Blumer and Haas, 2000). The reaction equation for cyanidation is shown in (1):4Au+8CN−+O2+2H2O=4AuCN2−+4OH− Obviously, cyanide concentration is quite important in gold leaching. However, Chi et al. (2011a, 2011b) reported that only a small amount of cyanide (3.5–15 mg/L) have been produced biologically, therefore, it is important work to improve cyanide concentration. Natarajan and Ting (2014) mentioned that two kinds of product was mainly generated by C.violaceum in the early stationary phase, one form was CN−, and the other was the non-dissociated form of HCN. The cyanide hydrolyzation process depends on the pH of the leaching conditions (Franco et al., 2016), and this argument is supported by a lot of researches. At physiological pH, cyanide mainly exists in the form of HCN (pKa 9.3). Cyanide is reduced to volatilize and cyanide ions is increased, when pH was above 9.3 (Young and Jordan, 1995). Above pH 10.5, the condition is suitable for cyanide production, but it is not suitable for cultivating microorganisms (Rees and Deventer, 1999; Shams et al., 2004). Under alkaline conditions (pH 8–10), cyanogenic microorganisms form a water-soluble metal cyanide complexes to leach the metals present in WPCBs scrap (Chi et al., 2011; Brandl et al., 2008; Faramarzi et al., 2004). Submission received: 24 February 2025 / Revised: 5 April 2025 / Accepted: 29 April 2025 / Published: 3 May 2025 Abstract The rapid consumption and disposal of electronic waste due to technological innovations and changes in living commodities are causing the development of a significant environmental challenge. Among the components of these wastes, spent printed circuit boards are particularly considered to be among the most valuable owing to their content of precious metals, such as gold first and potentially platinum, which may be available in a lower proportion. Effective methods as part of gold recovery strategies by industries and policymakers are developed and envisioned from economic and environmental perspectives. Currently, cyanidation dominates global gold production from e-waste due to its selectivity for gold. The high toxicity of cyanide, however, poses serious environmental issues, leading thiosulphate leaching to emerge as a non-toxic and promising alternative for gold extraction. Its industrial viability has been demonstrated by Barrick Gold Corporation at the Goldstrike site with the pretreatment of acidic or alkaline pressure oxidation. This review introduces bioleaching as a promising economic and environmentally friendly process for gold extraction. This review explores thiosulphate leaching of gold as an alternative to conventional cyanidation, with a particular focus on biothiosulphate production by adapted microorganisms. The factors that affect the pretreatment, chemical reaction mechanism, and design engineering are discussed. The consumption of thiosulphate was identified as one of the main challenges, restricting the reliability of the process. Various solutions for the reduction of its consumption and relevant process costs were discussed, with a particular examination from the engineering aspect of the process design and scalability to industrially relevant operating conditions by using bioreactors adapted to large pulp density loads of electrical waste. 1. Introduction Nowadays, the increasing reliance of the modern lifestyle on electronic devices with relatively short replacement cycles has led to a substantial rise in the accumulation of electrical waste (e-waste) [1]. According to statistics by [2], 40 million tons of e-waste are produced annually, which makes up around 5% of global solid waste. In 2019, Asia produced 46.6% of the world’s total e-waste, with America ranking the second highest with 24.4% e-waste generation followed by Europe (22.4%), Africa (5.4%), and Oceania (1.3%) [3]. Ref. [4] reported the production of 52.2 Mt global e-waste in 2021, which is expected to exceed 74.7 Mt by 2030 and 120 Mt by 2050. Despite this rise, only a proportion of 10–15% of generated e-waste is currently recycled, and the rest is stored or deposited in landfills, often with reduced strategies for sustainable recovery of the metals they contain, leading to unprecedented contamination of the environment and risks of diseases such as cancer, kidney and heart malfunctions, and brain swelling [5]. As a result, landfilling is considered the worst option as an e-waste destination, and there is an urgent need to recover metals from e-waste in order to mitigate environmental contamination, promote the economic advantages as a secondary source of precious metals, and save the consumption of natural ores [6]. Among e-waste, printed circuit boards (PCBs) contribute to approximately 3% of the total e-waste weight, while we note that mobile phones and computer PCBs have been widely studied owing to their high disposal volumes and precious metal contents [7]. They are utilised as random-access memory motherboards and network interface cards to facilitate electrical and mechanical connections, and their compositions can vary depending on the technology, year of fabrication, and manufacturer brand; however, they are typically composed of a metallic portion (40%) and non-metallic components such as plastics (30%) and ceramics (30%) [8]. They consist of a lamination layer of copper-clad fiberglass reinforced with epoxy resin material and other essential components such as capacitors, resistors, microchips, and diodes. The hazardous components of PCBs include heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd, As, and Cr), polychlorinated biphenyls, polybrominated biphenyls, and epoxy resins, which pose environmental challenges. Generally, PCBs contain about 10–20% Cu, 7% Fe, 5% Al, 3% Sn, 1–3% Ni, 1.5% Pb, 25% organic compounds, and precious metals such as 200–3000 ppm Ag, 20–250 ppm Au, and 10–200 ppm Pt, which are used because of their favourable electrical conductivity, chemical stability, and resistance to oxidation, corrosion, and acids [9]. The worth of Au and Ag in discarded PCBs in 2022 was estimated at USD 54,514.97/kg–USD 65,714.28/kg and USD 592.22/kg–USD 866.13/kg, respectively. Although their total weight is less than 1% of PCBs, they are still precious and financially important [10]. Every year, around 17 million PCBs are discarded, which is equivalent to the disposal of nearly 0.5 million tons of waste PCBs. In computer PCBs, the concentrations of Cu and Au reach 20–40 times and 25–250 times, respectively, more than natural ores, have the potential to be recovered from e-waste with less energy consumption, and are seen as alternative sources to natural ores [11]. As an example, 210 kg of Cu and 1.5 kg of Au can be recovered from one metric ton of waste PCBs, while only around 5 g and 5.25 kg of Au and Cu can be recovered from relevant natural ores, respectively [3]. fetched_contents.text: Bioleaching: urban mining option to curb the menace of E-waste challenge ABSTRACT Resource Recovery from Waste Electronics has emerged as one of the most imperative processes due to its pressing challenges all over the world. The Printed Circuit Board (PCB) is one of the typical E-waste components that comprise large varieties of metals and nonmetals. Urban Mining of these metals has received major attention all over the world. The existing treatment procedures used extensively for the resource extraction are hydrometallurgy and pyro-metallurgy and crude recycling practices in the informal sector. However, these methods are prone to cause secondary pollutants with certain drawbacks. Also, the existing informal recycling procedures resulted in insignificant occupational health hazards and severe environmental threats. The application of biotechnology is extensively exploited for metal extraction and emerged as one of the sustainable and eco-friendly tools. However, a limited field-scale study is prevailing in the realm of resource recovery from E-waste using bioleaching method. Hence, the application of bioleaching requires more attention and technical know-how in developing countries to curtail crude practices. The application of bioleaching in E-waste, including its available methods, kinetics mechanism associated opportunities, and barriers, have been discussed in this paper. A glance of E-waste management in India and the menace of 95% crude E-waste recycling are also elaborated. The incentives toward profit, socio-economic, and environmentally sustainable approaches have been delineated based on critical analysis of the available literature. fetched_contents.text: Comparative life cycle assessment of copper and gold recovery from waste printed circuit boards: Pyrometallurgy, chemical leaching and bioleaching Highlights * • Life cycle assessment of copper and gold recovery from waste printed circuit boards. * • Transparent life cycle inventory for pyro- and hydro-metallurgical processes. * • Pyrometallurgy has the lowest environmental impact with fossil-based electricity. * • Hydrometallurgy can have lowest global warming impact with carbon-free electricity. * • Metal recovery has lower environmental impact than primary production. Abstract Printed circuit boards (PCBs) make up a substantial amount of electronic waste (e-waste) generated annually. Waste PCBs contain high quantities of copper and gold in comparison to natural ores. As such, “urban mining” of waste PCBs to recover these metals is of commercial interest. In this work, we used life cycle assessment to compare the environmental impact of four copper and gold recovery processes. We evaluated pyrometallurgy, chemical leaching, and bioleaching, as well as a hybrid leaching process that uses bioleaching to recover copper and chemical leaching to recover gold. Furthermore, we considered differences in environmental impact based on differences in electricity sources. If electricity comes from fossil fuels, the pyrometallurgical process results in the lowest environmental impact in all impact categories studied. If electricity comes from carbon-free sources, the pyrometallurgical process results in the lowest environmental impact in all categories studied except global warming, where the hybrid leaching process results in the lowest impact. In all cases, metal recovery from waste PCBs leads to lower environmental impact than primary metal production. Our goal is to guide e-waste recyclers towards more environmentally sustainable metal recovery processes and to provide knowledge gaps in the field to guide future research. Introduction Consumer electronic products are immensely popular in contemporary society. This, combined with their short useful lives, has led to the generation of high quantities of electronic waste (e-waste) in recent years [1], [2]. Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are an essential component of nearly all electronics, and compose approximately 3–6 wt% of e-waste generated globally [2], [3], [4]. This waste stream contains a variety of valuable metals [5]. In particular, copper and gold are interesting to recover from waste PCBs due to the high mass of copper and high value of gold present in this waste stream [5]. PCBs contain approximately 20–40 times as much copper as typical copper ores and 25–250 times as much gold as typical gold ores [6], providing strong impetus for urban mining of waste PCBs to produce these metals. Many procedures exist for the recovery and purification of both copper and gold from waste PCBs. These can be classified as pyrometallurgical or hydrometallurgical [2], [5], [7], [8]. Pyrometallurgical techniques use heat to separate and purify metals. Hydrometallurgical techniques rely on dissolution of metals in aqueous solution and their subsequent recovery by either precipitation or electroplating [5]. Within the field of hydrometallurgical processing, biohydrometallurgical techniques are becoming increasingly popular in the research community [9]. While conventional hydrometallurgical techniques use synthetic chemicals to dissolve metals, biohydrometallurgical techniques use chemicals generated by microorganisms [10]. From here, we differentiate hydrometallurgical techniques as either bioleaching or chemical leaching whereby the processes rely on microbiologically derived or synthetic chemicals, respectively. Various authors have made qualitative claims about the relative environmental impact of these three methods, but these claims are not always corroborated by quantitative environmental impact assessment such as life cycle assessment (LCA). For example, reviews by Baniasadi et al. [9] and Priya and Hait [10] noted that bioleaching for metal recovery has lower environmental impact in comparison to conventional techniques for metal recovery (pyrometallurgy and chemical leaching). Hsu et al. [8] and Dutta et al. [4] also claim that hydrometallurgical techniques have lower environmental impact in comparison to pyrometallurgical techniques. These qualitative assessments are sometimes contradicted by quantitative LCA studies comparing the environmental impact of different metal recovery procedures. For example, an LCA study by Villares et al. [6] found that bioleaching to recover copper resulted in significantly greater environmental impact in all categories when compared to recovery of copper by pyrometallurgy. LCA and techno-economic analysis by Işildar [11] compared three processes for copper and gold recovery: (1) copper and gold recovery by bioleaching, (2) copper and gold recovery by chemical leaching, and (3) copper recovery by bioleaching and gold recovery by chemical leaching. The results showed that gold bioleaching was not economically feasible due to the low yield of 34 % for gold bioleaching (process 1) in comparison to 75 % yield for gold chemical leaching (processes 2 and 3). This stark difference in yield makes it difficult to compare the environmental impact of gold recovery by these processes. When comparing copper recovery by bioleaching (process 3) and by chemical leaching (process 2), Işildar found that there were clear tradeoffs in different environmental impact categories, such that neither process had the lowest environmental impact in all categories studied. The qualitative claims mentioned previously are also sometimes corroborated by quantitative assessment. For example, Li et al. node_outputs.N8:
Why PCB composition and waste variability matter for bioleaching effectiveness

PCB composition is central to bioleaching performance because waste PCBs are not chemically uniform and contain both metals and non-metal components that influence leaching behavior. The evidence shows that PCBs are composed of metallic portions, non-metallic components such as plastics and ceramics, and a lamination layer of copper-clad fiberglass reinforced with epoxy resin, plus capacitors, resistors, microchips, and diodes [N1-F2]. They also contain hazardous components such as heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd, As, Cr), polychlorinated biphenyls, polybrominated biphenyls, and epoxy resins [N1-F2]. In addition, PCBs are described as typically containing about 10–20% Cu, 7% Fe, 5% Al, 3% Sn, 1–3% Ni, 1.5% Pb, 25% organic compounds, and precious metals such as 200–3000 ppm Ag and 20–250 ppm Au [N1-F2]. This heterogeneous composition means that bioleaching must deal with a complex matrix of metals and non-metals, rather than a simple mineral ore.

The non-metal components matter because PCBs are not purely metallic. The evidence explicitly notes that PCBs consist of plastics, ceramics, and other non-metallic materials [N1-F2], and that PCB waste includes organic compounds and potentially toxic organic residues such as epoxy resins and brominated flame retardants [N1-F2]. These organic components can interfere with leaching and may require pretreatment, because the evidence shows that pretreatment can significantly improve gold leaching rates [N1-F2]. The presence of plastics, ceramics, and organic matter also increases the likelihood of contamination and complicates recovery, because the bioleaching process must separate and extract metals from a matrix that is not a clean ore [N1-F2].

Crushed PCB particle size and surface area are important because bioleaching efficiency depends on the amount of exposed surface area available for microbial action. The evidence states that PCBs are crushed and milled into small sizes, such as 0.5 mm, before dissolution [N2-R5]. The same source suggests that particle size reduction is a standard pretreatment step in PCB recycling [N2-R5]. Smaller particle size increases surface area, which can improve contact between microbes and the metal-bearing material, but it also increases the complexity of the waste stream and may make separation more difficult [N2-R5]. In bioleaching, smaller particles are generally favorable because they increase the effective contact area for microbial attack and solubilization, but the evidence here does not quantify particle size effects directly; it only shows that crushing is a common preprocessing step [N2-R5].

Interferences from other metals and organic residues are a key limitation. The evidence indicates that PCBs contain multiple metals such as copper, iron, aluminum, tin, nickel, lead, and precious metals [N1-F2]. In bioleaching, the presence of multiple metals can create competition for microbial activity and may lower gold recovery because the system must selectively recover gold from a complex mixture [N1-F2]. The evidence also notes that PCBs contain organic compounds and epoxy resins, which may act as contaminants or interfere with microbial performance [N1-F2]. Moreover, the PCB toxicity described in the bioleaching literature suggests that the waste stream itself can be harmful to microbial growth, which is an important practical constraint [N4-F4]. The review explicitly states that PCB toxicity can limit microbial performance and that bioleaching is recommended for gold recovery compared to other processes, but it also notes that the existing literature is limited in field-scale study [N4-F4]. In short, PCB composition and waste variability matter because they create a heterogeneous, contaminated, and multi-metal matrix that complicates bioleaching and requires pretreatment, careful process control, and careful selection of microbes and conditions [N1-F2][N2-R5][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N7:
What the available evidence says about how effective bioleaching is for PCB gold recovery

The evidence suggests that bioleaching can be effective for PCB gold recovery, but the reported recovery rates vary by study and process, and the evidence base is mixed in terms of lab, pilot, and field-scale demonstration. Direct evidence indicates that gold bioleaching from PCBs is being studied as a promising alternative to traditional cyanide-based methods [N1-F1][N1-F2]. One review states that bioleaching is regarded as a promising technology for recycling metals due to its environmental friendliness and low cost [N1-F1]. Another review notes that bioleaching is increasingly applied to recover valuable metals from e-waste [N1-F2].

On reported recovery rates, the evidence is not uniformly high. A recent review cites that pretreatment can improve gold leaching from PCBs, with one example showing that the Au leaching rate increased from 20.8% before pretreatment to 40.1% after pretreatment [N1-F2]. Another study reports over 70% bioleaching efficiency of gold by Kumar et al. (2021), using C. violaceum and bacterial strains [N1-R4]. The same review also states that 210 kg of Cu and 1.5 kg of Au can be recovered from one metric ton of waste PCBs [N1-F2]. This is important because it shows that PCBs are highly metal-rich waste streams, and bioleaching can recover meaningful amounts of gold and copper, but it does not necessarily translate into a universally high single-recovery rate for gold alone [N1-F2].

The evidence also indicates that PCB composition and gold form affect recovery. PCBs are described as containing about 20–250 ppm Au, along with other metals and organic materials [N1-F2]. This suggests that gold is not always present in a highly concentrated, easily leachable form, and that recovery depends on the metal matrix. The evidence further shows that pretreatment can improve recovery, implying that the gold may be embedded or partially protected within the PCB structure [N1-F2]. The PCB composition evidence also notes that PCBs contain high concentrations of copper, iron, aluminum, tin, nickel, and lead, along with precious metals such as silver and gold [N1-F2]. This supports the idea that gold recovery is part of a broader metal recovery effort from PCBs, and that bioleaching must contend with a complex mixture rather than a pure gold ore [N1-F2].

Conditions and process parameters that improve recovery are clearly relevant. The evidence shows that pulp density affects bioleaching efficiency; one study reported that gold bioleaching efficiency decreased with increasing pulp density and that 0.33% w/v pulp density was used in that work [N1-R1]. This is important because it demonstrates that process parameters can strongly influence recovery. The same review also notes that pretreatment can significantly increase leaching rates [N1-F2]. Another source indicates that bioleaching performance is influenced by pH, solid concentration, energy source, agitation rate, irrigation rate, aeration rate, and other operating conditions [N4-R4]. This supports the conclusion that bioleaching is not a single-recipe process; it is sensitive to a range of parameters, including pH control and aeration [N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that pretreatment can improve recovery, which implies that pretreatment is a key step for improving gold leaching from PCBs [N1-F2].

In summary, the available evidence suggests bioleaching can be effective for PCB gold recovery, but the reported recovery rates are not uniformly high across all studies, and they are often lab- or pilot-scale results rather than fully field-validated processes [N1-F2][N1-R4]. PCB gold recovery is more likely to be effective when the material is pretreated, when pulp density is carefully controlled, and when other operating conditions such as pH and aeration are optimized [N1-R1][N1-F2][N4-R4]. The evidence also shows that PCBs are highly metal-rich and heterogeneous, so recovery depends on both the gold form and the broader PCB composition [N1-F2].
node_outputs.N9:
Practical limitations and why bioleaching may not be the best option

Bioleaching has several practical limitations that make it less attractive in some settings, despite its environmental appeal. One major limitation is slow kinetics and long processing times. The evidence shows that bioleaching performance is influenced by pH, solid concentration, energy source, agitation rate, irrigation rate, aeration rate, and other operating conditions [N4-R4]. This implies that the process is not fast by nature and may require extended contact times to achieve acceptable recovery. The review also states that pretreatment can improve recovery, which suggests that the system is not inherently efficient and that additional steps are often needed [N1-F2]. In the context of PCB recovery, where waste streams are complex and time-sensitive, slow kinetics may reduce practical attractiveness.

Energy and cost tradeoffs are another key limitation. The evidence indicates that bioleaching is marketed as a low-cost and environmentally friendly alternative to conventional methods [N1-F1], but it also notes that comparative life cycle assessment results show gold bioleaching was not economically feasible in one study due to a low yield of 34% for gold bioleaching compared to 75% for gold chemical leaching [N5-F3]. This is an important contradiction: bioleaching may have lower direct chemical costs, but it may not be economically viable if yields are low or if operational requirements increase costs. The evidence also highlights that bioleaching is highly recommended for gold recovery compared to other processes, but the same review notes that there is a limited field-scale study and that PCB toxicity can limit microbial performance [N4-F4]. This combination of limited field validation, low yields, and toxicity-related constraints suggests that bioleaching may not be the best option when high throughput and reliability are required.

Contamination, pH control, and reagent requirements are practical challenges. The PCB waste matrix is heterogeneous and contains multiple metals and organic residues [N1-F2], which can interfere with selective gold recovery. The evidence also notes that PCB toxicity can limit microbial performance, which directly affects contamination control [N4-F4]. Bioleaching typically requires careful pH control, as the evidence shows that bioleaching performance is influenced by pH and that cyanide-producing bacteria operate optimally in specific pH ranges [N1-F1][N4-R4]. In addition, bioleaching may require reagents or pretreatment steps, which can add cost and complexity [N1-F2]. The review explicitly states that pretreatment can improve gold leaching rates, implying that the process is not self-contained and may depend on complementary steps [N1-F2].

Compared with other PCB recycling methods, bioleaching has both advantages and disadvantages. The evidence states that bioleaching is regarded as promising because it is environmentally friendly and low-cost [N1-F1], and that it is increasingly applied to recover valuable metals from e-waste [N1-F2]. However, comparative life cycle assessment results show that pyrometallurgy can have the lowest environmental impact when electricity comes from fossil fuels, while hydrometallurgy can have lower global warming impact with carbon-free electricity [N5-F3]. Another study found that gold bioleaching was not economically feasible due to its low yield [N5-F3]. This suggests that bioleaching may be less attractive than chemical leaching in terms of yield and economics, and that pyrometallurgy may have advantages in certain environmental contexts [N5-F3]. Overall, bioleaching may not be the best option when the goal is high recovery speed, high yield, or low cost, because it is slower, has limited field validation, and is sensitive to contamination, pH, and pretreatment requirements [N4-R4][N5-F3][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Economic and environmental implications of using bioleaching for PCB gold recovery

The economic and environmental implications of bioleaching for PCB gold recovery are mixed. On the economic side, the evidence shows that bioleaching is often presented as low-cost and environmentally friendly [N1-F1], but comparative economic feasibility is not uniform. A life cycle assessment study found that gold bioleaching was not economically feasible due to a low yield of 34% for gold bioleaching compared to 75% for gold chemical leaching [N5-F3]. This is a strong economic limitation: even if bioleaching has low direct chemical costs, its poor yield can make it economically unattractive. The review also notes that pretreatment can improve recovery, which implies that additional capital and operational costs may be needed to achieve acceptable yields [N1-F2]. The evidence further suggests that bioleaching may require careful process control and pretreatment, which can add to capital and operational costs [N1-F2][N4-R4]. Overall, bioleaching may be economically feasible only when yields are high enough and when the cost of pretreatment and process control is offset by environmental or secondary benefits [N5-F3].

On the environmental side, bioleaching can offer benefits but also carries risks. The evidence states that bioleaching is an environmentally friendly and cost-effective technique for extracting metals from low-grade ores and waste materials [N3-R2]. It is also described as a promising alternative to conventional cyanidation, especially because thiosulphate leaching is non-toxic and has industrial viability [N1-F2]. However, the same evidence notes that the process has limited field-scale study and that PCB toxicity can limit microbial performance [N4-F4]. This means that while bioleaching can reduce some chemical toxicity compared to cyanide, it is not necessarily free of environmental risk. The review also highlights that bioleaching is part of a broader urban mining strategy to curb e-waste, but that PCB waste streams are complex and can generate secondary pollutants [N4-F4].
